trap.wrong: "Store every user id in a set and count it" or "SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)."
trap.why: Exact distinct counts and top-K over billions of events need memory proportional to the number of distinct items and are expensive to merge across time ranges. Most product uses tolerate about 1% error.
trap.probe: Whether you know probabilistic data structures and when approximation is acceptable.
trap.say: "For dashboards I'd use HyperLogLog for distinct counts and count-min sketch or heavy-hitter algorithms for top-K, with a few KB per counter and around 1% error, and keep exact counts only where money depends on them."

thesis: When the question is 'about how many' or 'which are the biggest', probabilistic structures give small, mergeable answers with bounded error: HyperLogLog for distinct counts, count-min sketch and heavy-hitter algorithms for frequencies and top-K, Bloom filters for membership. Use exact counting only where correctness matters.
pitch: Exact unique counts need to remember every id seen, which at billions of events means huge memory, and combining days means unioning huge sets. HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts using a few kilobytes per counter with a standard error around 1%, and two HLLs can be merged, so daily sketches combine into weekly or monthly counts cheaply. For top-K, a count-min sketch estimates frequencies in fixed memory, possibly overestimating, and algorithms like Space-Saving track heavy hitters directly. Bloom filters answer 'have I seen this before?' with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate. I'd ask first whether approximation is acceptable: dashboard unique visitors and trending items, yes; billing, ad spend and payouts, no, or at least reconciled with exact batch counts. Redis, Druid, BigQuery and many warehouses ship these structures built in.

points.d: Product analytics and trending usually tolerate small errors; billing and payouts don't.
Fixed small memory, roughly 1% standard error at typical settings, mergeable across shards and time windows.
Fixed memory, estimates never undercount, error bounded by width and depth. Good for 'how often' queries.
Space-Saving or count-min plus a heap tracks the most frequent items in bounded memory.
Check 'seen before?' with no false negatives and configurable false positives; useful for dedupe and avoiding needless lookups.
Redis (PFADD/PFCOUNT), warehouses (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT) and stream processors provide these; avoid writing your own.

decision: Approximate structures for analytics, trending and dedupe at scale; exact counting (often batch, reconciled) for anything financial or contractual.
numbers: Redis HyperLogLog uses at most about 12 KB per key and has a standard error of 0.81%.
Exact distinct count of 1 billion 8-byte ids needs roughly 8 GB just for the ids, before set overhead.
pitfalls: Summing HLL estimates instead of merging sketches, which double-counts overlapping users.
Bloom filters sized for today's volume, whose false-positive rate climbs as items grow.
COUNT(DISTINCT) over raw events on every dashboard load.

followups.q: How do you get weekly uniques from daily counts?
followups.a: Store a daily HyperLogLog sketch and merge seven of them; adding the daily numbers would double-count returning users.

followups.q: How do you dedupe events with a Bloom filter safely?
followups.a: Use it as a fast pre-check; on a possible duplicate, confirm against an exact store if a false positive would drop a real event.

followups.q: When is exact counting still needed in streaming?
followups.a: Ad billing, payouts and quotas. Count exactly in a batch or with idempotent keyed aggregates and reconcile with the streaming estimate.

example: A content platform replaced per-article exact unique-reader sets (tens of GB in Redis) with per-article daily HyperLogLogs (about 12 KB each). Monthly uniques are now a merge of 30 sketches, accurate within about 1%, and memory fell by over 99%.
